# Estimating High Order Gradients of the Data Distribution by Denoising
## Introduction
In machine learning, the "score" of a distribution—the first-order gradient of its log-density ($\nabla \log p(x)$)—has become a cornerstone for generative modeling (such as Stable Diffusion) and denoising applications. However, first-order information only tells us the "direction" of the data. Higher-order derivatives, like the Hessian, provide critical information about the **curvature** and local structure of the data distribution, unlocking new capabilities in uncertainty quantification and accelerated sampling.
## The Bottleneck of Higher-Order Scores
The authors sought a way to learn these higher-order scores directly from noisy samples, mirroring how we learn first-order scores via Denoising Score Matching (DSM).
## Direct Estimation via Tweedie's Formula
The researchers' key insight stems from a deep connection between Denoising Score Matching and **Tweedie’s formula**, a classic result in Bayesian statistics that relates the first-order score to the posterior mean of a clean sample given a noisy one.
The authors generalized this formula to higher-order moments, proving that the $n$-th order moment of the posterior distribution can be expressed as a polynomial of scores up to order $n$. By setting up a least-squares regression problem where a neural network predicts these moments from noisy data, the model implicitly and directly learns the high-order scores.
## Key Insights and Results
- **Uncertainty Quantification:** The second-order score is mathematically linked to the covariance of the clean data given a noisy observation. This means the Hessian captures the "ambiguity" of a denoising task. By visualizing the eigenvectors of the estimated covariance on MNIST, the authors showed how a noisy '4' could potentially be a '9', providing a powerful qualitative tool for understanding model doubt.

This view is also consistent with (but by no means required by) the results of Galton and Einstein. In the first attempts to apply probability theory in the biological and social sciences (for example, Quetelet, 1835, 1869), serious errors were made through supposing firstly that the appearance of a normal distribution in data indicates that one is sampling from a homogeneous population, and secondly that any departure from normality indicates an inhomogeneity in need of explanation. By resolving a non-normal distribution into Gaussians, Quetelet thought that one would be discovering the different sub-species, or varieties, that were present in the population. If this were true reliably, we would indeed have a powerful tool for research in many different fields. But later study showed that the situation is not that simple. We have just seen how one aspect of it was corrected finally by Galton (1886), in showing that a normal frequency distribution by no means proves homogeneity; from (7.73), a Gaussian of width σ can arise inhomogeneously – and in many different ways – from the overlapping of narrower Gaussian distributions of various widths σ1 , σ2 . But those subpopulations are in general merely mathematical artifacts like the sine waves in a Fourier transform; they have no individual significance for the phenomenon unless one can show that a particular set of subpopulations has a real existence and plays a real part in the mechanism underlying stability and change. # Sum-of-squares lower bounds for Non-Gaussian Component Analysis

Non-Gaussian Component Analysis (NGCA) is the statistical task of finding a non-Gaussian direction in a high-dimensional dataset. Specifically, given i.i.d.\ samples from a distribution $P^A_{v}$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ that behaves like a known distribution $A$ in a hidden direction $v$ and like a standard Gaussian in the orthogonal complement, the goal is to approximate the hidden direction. The standard formulation posits that the first $k-1$ moments of $A$ match those of the standard Gaussian and the $k$-th moment differs. Under mild assumptions, this problem has sample complexity $O(n)$. On the other hand, all known efficient algorithms require $\Omega(n^{k/2})$ samples. Prior work developed sharp Statistical Query and low-degree testing lower bounds suggesting an information-computation tradeoff for this problem. Here we study the complexity of NGCA in the Sum-of-Squares (SoS) framework. Our main contribution is the first super-constant degree SoS lower bound for NGCA. Specifically, we show that if the non-Gaussian distribution $A$ matches the first $(k-1)$ moments of $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ and satisfies other mild conditions, then with fewer than $n^{(1 - \varepsilon)k/2}$ many samples from the normal distribution, with high probability, degree $(\log n)^{{1\over 2}-o_n(1)}$ SoS fails to refute the existence of such a direction $v$. Our result significantly strengthens prior work by establishing a super-polynomial information-computation tradeoff against a broader family of algorithms. As corollaries, we obtain SoS lower bounds for several problems in robust statistics and the learning of mixture models. Our SoS lower bound proof introduces a novel technique, that we believe may be of broader interest, and a number of refinements over existing methods.

摘要

Non-Gaussian component analysis (NGCA) is a problem in multidimensional data analysis which, since its formulation in 2006, has attracted considerable attention in statistics and machine learning. In this problem, we have a random variable X in n -dimensional Euclidean space. There is an unknown subspace Γ of the n -dimensional Euclidean space such that the orthogonal projection of X onto Γ is standard multidimensional Gaussian and the orthogonal projection of X onto Γ ⊥ , the orthogonal complement of Γ, is non-Gaussian, in the sense that all its one-dimensional marginals are different from the Gaussian in a certain metric defined in terms of moments. The NGCA problem is to approximate the non-Gaussian subspace Γ ⊥ given samples of X . Vectors in Γ ⊥ correspond to ‘interesting’ directions, whereas vectors in Γ correspond to the directions where data is very noisy. The most interesting applications of the NGCA model is for the case when the magnitude of the noise is comparable to that of the true signal, a setting in which traditional noise reduction techniques such as PCA don’t apply directly. NGCA is also related to dimension reduction and to other data analysis problems such as ICA. NGCA-like problems have been studied in statistics for a long time using techniques such as projection pursuit. We give an algorithm that takes polynomial time in the dimension n and has an inverse polynomial dependence on the error parameter measuring the angle distance between the non-Gaussian subspace and the subspace output by the algorithm. Our algorithm is based on relative entropy as the contrast function and fits under the projection pursuit framework. The techniques we develop for analyzing our algorithm maybe of use for other related problems.

## Abstract

We study score learning from denoising pairs with a hidden non-Gaussian component. In one regime covariance reveals it; in another, isotropic covariance hides it until the first distinguishing moment, of order $k^{\ast}$. ###### Abstract

While diffusion models have emerged as a powerful class of generative models, their learning dynamics remain poorly understood. We address this issue first by empirically showing that standard diffusion models trained on natural images exhibit a distributional simplicity bias, learning simple, pair-wise input statistics before specializing to higher-order correlations. We reproduce this behaviour in simple denoisers trained on a minimal data model, the mixed cumulant model, where we precisely control both pair-wise and higher-order correlations of the inputs. keenable.snippet:
> Abstract:Non-Gaussian Component Analysis (NGCA) is the statistical task of finding a non-Gaussian direction in a high-dimensional dataset. Specifically, given i.i.d.\ samples from a distribution $P^A_{v}$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ that behaves like a known distribution $A$ in a hidden direction $v$ and like a standard Gaussian in the orthogonal complement, the goal is to approximate the hidden direction. The standard formulation posits that the first $k-1$ moments of $A$ match those of the standard Gaussian and the $k$-th moment differs. Under mild assumptions, this problem has sample complexity $O(n)$. On the other hand, all known efficient algorithms require $\Omega(n^{k/2})$ samples. Prior work developed sharp Statistical Query and low-degree testing lower bounds suggesting an information-computation tradeoff for this problem.
> Here we study the complexity of NGCA in the Sum-of-Squares (SoS) framework. Our main contribution is the first super-constant degree SoS lower bound for NGCA. Specifically, we show that if the non-Gaussian distribution $A$ matches the first $(k-1)$ moments of $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ and satisfies other mild conditions, then with fewer than $n^{(1 - \varepsilon)k/2}$ many samples from the normal distribution, with high probability, degree $(\log n)^{{1\over 2}-o_n(1)}$ SoS fails to refute the existence of such a direction $v$. Our result significantly strengthens prior work by establishing a super-polynomial information-computation tradeoff against a broader family of algorithms. As corollaries, we obtain SoS lower bounds for several problems in robust statistics and the learning of mixture models.

keenable-realtime.snippet:
> Abstract:Non-Gaussian Component Analysis (NGCA) is the statistical task of finding a non-Gaussian direction in a high-dimensional dataset. Specifically, given i.i.d.\ samples from a distribution $P^A_{v}$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ that behaves like a known distribution $A$ in a hidden direction $v$ and like a standard Gaussian in the orthogonal complement, the goal is to approximate the hidden direction. The standard formulation posits that the first $k-1$ moments of $A$ match those of the standard Gaussian and the $k$-th moment differs. Under mild assumptions, this problem has sample complexity $O(n)$. On the other hand, all known efficient algorithms require $\Omega(n^{k/2})$ samples. Prior work developed sharp Statistical Query and low-degree testing lower bounds suggesting an information-computation tradeoff for this problem.
> Here we study the complexity of NGCA in the Sum-of-Squares (SoS) framework. Our main contribution is the first super-constant degree SoS lower bound for NGCA. Specifically, we show that if the non-Gaussian distribution $A$ matches the first $(k-1)$ moments of $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ and satisfies other mild conditions, then with fewer than $n^{(1 - \varepsilon)k/2}$ many samples from the normal distribution, with high probability, degree $(\log n)^{{1\over 2}-o_n(1)}$ SoS fails to refute the existence of such a direction $v$. Our result significantly strengthens prior work by establishing a super-polynomial information-computation tradeoff against a broader family of algorithms. As corollaries, we obtain SoS lower bounds for several problems in robust statistics and the learning of mixture models.

octen.snippet:
Abstract
Most conventional techniques for independent component analysis (or blind source separation) resort to second-order statistics to decorrelate the observed data. The prewhitening step makes these algorithms sensitive to the presence of additive Gaussian noise. A higher-order-only technique is presented. The identification problem is approached in a (linear and multilinear) algebraic framework: our derivation starts with the observation that the solution can be obtained from the canonical decomposition (CANDECOMP) of a higher-order cumulant tensor. Next, it is demonstrated that the CANDECOMP components follow from the simultaneous diagonalization, by congruence transformation, of a set of matrices. A reformulation in terms of orthogonal unknowns leads to a simultaneous Schur decomposition, which is solved by a Givens-type iteration. The technique can be considered as the higher-order-only equivalent of the popular JADE-algorithm.

octen.snippet:
Learning from higher-order correlations, efficiently: hypothesis tests, random features, and neural networks
Neural networks excel at discovering statistical patterns in high-dimensional data sets. In practice, higher-order cumulants, which quantify the non-Gaussian correlations between three or more variables, are particularly important for the performance of neural networks. But how efficient are neural networks at extracting features from higher-order cumulants? We study this question in the spiked cumulant model, where the statistician needs to recover a privileged direction or "spike'' from the order-$p\ge 4$ cumulants of $d$-dimensional inputs. We first discuss the fundamental statistical and computational limits of recovering the spike by analysing the number of samples $n$ required to strongly distinguish between inputs from the spiked cumulant model and isotropic Gaussian inputs. Existing literature established the presence of a wide statistical-to-computational gap in this problem. We deepen this line of work by finding an exact formula for the likelihood ratio norm which proves that statistical distinguishability requires $n\gtrsim d$ samples, while distinguishing the two distributions in polynomial time requires $n \gtrsim d^2$ samples for a wide class of algorithms, i.e. those covered by the low-degree conjecture. Numerical experiments show that neural networks do indeed learn to distinguish the two distributions with quadratic sample complexity, while ``lazy'' methods like random features are not better than random guessing in this regime. Our results show that neural networks extract information from higher-order correlations in the spiked cumulant model efficiently, and reveal a large gap in the amount of data required by neural networks and random features to learn from higher-order cumulants.

octen.title: Beyond PCA: Statistical and Computational Limits of Higher-Order Spectral Methods - Department of Statistics and Data Science
octen.snippet:
Beyond PCA: Statistical and Computational Limits of Higher-Order Spectral Methods
 
MING YUAN – COLUMBIA UNIVERSITY 
ABSTRACT
Spectral methods are fundamental tools in statistics, underlying PCA, factor models, and many approaches to latent structure recovery. But oftentimes second-order information is not enough, and the relevant structure appears only in higher-order moments. In this talk, I will use tensor spectral methods to explore this question, with independent component analysis as a motivating example. Higher-order structure leads to several phenomena that differ sharply from familiar matrix theory: individual components can remain identifiable even without spectral gaps, and they can often be estimated much more accurately than the full higher-order moment itself. These properties also open the door to statistical inference for the recovered components. On the computational side, simple iterative algorithms can achieve optimal statistical accuracy once properly initialized, but finding a good initialization can be substantially harder. This creates a fundamental gap between what is statistically possible and what can be achieved efficiently. The talk will highlight connections among PCA, ICA, high-dimensional estimation, and computation, and illustrate how moving beyond second-order methods can change both the statistical and computational landscape.

octen.snippet:
Like the ordinary power spectrum, higher-order spectra (HOS) describe signal
properties that are invariant under translations in time. Unlike the power
spectrum, HOS retain phase information from which details of the signal
waveform can be recovered. Here we consider the problem of identifying multiple
unknown transient waveforms which recur within an ensemble of records at
mutually random delays. We develop a new technique for recovering filters from
HOS whose performance in waveform detection approaches that of an optimal
matched filter, requiring no prior information about the waveforms. Unlike
previous techniques of signal identification through HOS, the method applies
equally well to signals with deterministic and non-deterministic HOS. In the
non-deterministic case, it yields an additive decomposition, introducing a new
approach to the separation of component processes within non-Gaussian signals
having non-deterministic higher moments. We show a close relationship to
minimum-entropy blind deconvolution (MED), which the present technique improves
upon by avoiding the need for numerical optimization, while requiring only
numerically stable operations of time shift, element-wise multiplication and
averaging, making it particularly suited for real-time applications. The
application of HOS decomposition to real-world signals is demonstrated with
blind denoising, detection and classification of normal and abnormal heartbeats
in electrocardiograms. eess.SP, q-bio.QM, stat.AP Christopher K. Kovach, M. A. Howard

[Submitted on 2 Nov 2026]

Title: Denoising Is Stein: Moment Access and a Resource Hierarchy for Learning Hidden Structure in Diffusion Models

Authors: Rui Wang
View PDF HTML (experimental)
Abstract: We study score learning from denoising pairs when the data contain a hidden non-Gaussian component. If covariance reveals the component, its subspace can be recovered directly. If covariance is isotropic, the first distinguishing moment has order $k^\ast$, and the learner must extract that moment from clean points and their noisy views. Correlations in the denoising loss are Stein discrepancies against a baseline; for polynomial fields they determine exactly the corresponding moment differences. Averaging fresh noisy views conditional on a clean point gives an exact moment query on the clean distribution. In the covariance-matched regime, orientation-independent dictionaries satisfying an $L^4/L^2$ condition need order $d^{k^\ast-1}$ features, and the stated dot-product kernel ridge models need the same power in samples. Small-step online SGD on one unit has this exponent up to logarithms. A two-stage learner uses the curvature of a smoothed denoising loss to recover the hidden direction, then sharpens it and fits a scalar readout. For every even $k^\ast$, it obtains a fixed score gain over the Gaussian baseline from $O(d^{k^\ast/2}\log d)$ clean points. In the covariance-visible regime, the frozen-feature threshold occurs at $d^J/J!$, while projection onto principal components makes the fitted-model, score-risk and generated-law distributions independent of ambient dimension. In the covariance-matched experiments, the measured partial-trace overlaps are consistent with the proposed spectral transition. A width-8 network trained with clean-point reuse shows a $d^2$-like training-set threshold over $d=64$--$192$, with fixed validation and calibration overhead.

parallel.snippet:
## Abstract

Non-Gaussian component analysis (NGCA) is a problem in multidimensional data analysis which, since its formulation in 2006, has attracted considerable attention in statistics and machine learning. In this problem, we have a random variable _X_ in _n_ \-dimensional Euclidean space. There is an unknown subspace Γ of the _n_ \-dimensional Euclidean space such that the orthogonal projection of _X_ onto Γ is standard multidimensional Gaussian and the orthogonal projection of _X_ onto Γ ⊥ , the orthogonal complement of Γ, is non-Gaussian, in the sense that all its one-dimensional marginals are different from the Gaussian in a certain metric defined in terms of moments. The NGCA problem is to approximate the non-Gaussian subspace Γ ⊥ given samples of _X_ .

Vectors in Γ ⊥ correspond to ‘interesting’ directions, whereas vectors in Γ correspond to the directions where data is very noisy. The most interesting applications of the NGCA model is for the case when the magnitude of the noise is comparable to that of the true signal, a setting in which traditional noise reduction techniques such as PCA don’t apply directly. NGCA is also related to dimension reduction and to other data analysis problems such as ICA. NGCA-like problems have been studied in statistics for a long time using techniques such as projection pursuit.

We give an algorithm that takes polynomial time in the dimension _n_ and has an inverse polynomial dependence on the error parameter measuring the angle distance between the non-Gaussian subspace and the subspace output by the algorithm. Our algorithm is based on relative entropy as the contrast function and fits under the projection pursuit framework. The techniques we develop for analyzing our algorithm maybe of use for other related problems.

# Sample complexity bounds for learning high-dimensional simplices in noisy regimes
## Abstract
In this paper, we find a sample complexity bound for learning a simplex from noisy samples.
Assume a dataset of size *n* is given which includes i.i.d. samples drawn from a uniform distribution over an unknown simplex in R*^K^*, where samples are assumed to be corrupted by a multivariate additive Gaussian noise of an arbitrary magnitude.
We prove the existence of an algorithm that with high probability outputs a simplex having a ℓ~2~-distance of at most ε from the true simplex (for any ε > 0).
Also, we theoretically show that in order to achieve this bound, it is sufficient to have *n* ≥ (*K* ^2^/ε^2^) (*e* ^Ω(*K*/SNR2)^ samples, where SNR stands for the signal-to-noise ratio.
This result solves an open problem in this area of research and shows as long as SNR ≥ Ω (*K* ^1/2^), the sample complexity of the noisy regime has the same order to that of the noiseless case.
Our proofs are a combination of the so-called sample compression technique from (Ashtiani et al., 2018), mathematical tools from high-dimensional geometry, and Fourier analysis.
In particular, we have proposed a general Fourier-based technique for recovery of a more general class of distribution families from additive Gaussian noise, which can be further used in a variety of other related problems.

# Sample complexity bounds for learning high-dimensional simplices in noisy regimes
## Abstract
In this paper, we find a sample complexity bound for learning a simplex from noisy samples.
Assume a dataset of size *n* is given which includes i.i.d. samples drawn from a uniform distribution over an unknown simplex in R*^K^*, where samples are assumed to be corrupted by a multivariate additive Gaussian noise of an arbitrary magnitude.
We prove the existence of an algorithm that with high probability outputs a simplex having a ℓ~2~-distance of at most ε from the true simplex (for any ε > 0).

seltz.snippet:
An image generator starts with an array of numbers that look like random noise and keeps changing that array until it lands somewhere near the distribution of images a prompt describes. Diffusion training makes that possible by running the process backward first: take real images and wreck them, adding ordinary bell-curve noise — Gaussian noise — in small steps whose sizes you chose in advance. Because you know exactly how much you added at every step, you can train a network to point back toward the clean version. Flow matching skips the wrecking story and learns a velocity field instead: for any point, which direction to move and how fast. Both are describing transport — moving probability mass from a simple source to structured data.

This drawing keeps one two-dimensional distribution in the same coordinates across every sheet, deliberately small enough that you can look at it. Forward noise, reverse denoising, compression, guidance, numerical sampling, probability flow, and flow matching all act on those same points. A real image model works in thousands or millions of dimensions and learns from image-text data, so what the toy explains is geometry — never output quality.

The lineage runs from denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs), through classifier-free guidance and latent diffusion, out to Diffusion Transformers (DiT) and flow matching. Architectures and product defaults will keep changing. What survives is the pair of endpoint distributions, a time-dependent field, conditioning, a numerical solver, and the representation the path gets learned in.

seltz.snippet: Imagine you want to generate realistic images. Instead of learning the probability of each image directly, you learn something subtler. You learn which direction in pixel space makes an image *more likely*. This direction field, called the **score**, is the gradient of the log-density of the data distribution. If you had this field everywhere, you could start from random noise. You would simply "walk uphill" toward regions of high probability. This arrives at realistic samples. This is the central idea behind score-based generative modeling. It is a framework that unifies denoising autoencoders, Langevin dynamics, and Diffusion Models: Forward and Reverse Processes into one coherent mathematical story. The practical obstacle is that the true score of real data is unknown. The density itself is intractable to normalize. Computing it directly would require an impossible integral over all of image space. Score-based models sidestep this by learning to estimate the score using only samples. They do this via an objective called **score matching**. This objective remarkably never needs the normalizing constant at all. A key insight, due to Vincent's denoising score matching, shows something important. Training a network to denoise noisy data is *mathematically equivalent* to training it to estimate the score of the noised distribution. This connects an easy, well-posed regression problem — predict the noise that was added — to the deep theoretical object of a score field. This equivalence matters enormously in practice. They are trained with a denoising objective that implicitly estimates a score function at many noise scales. ### What a generative model learns

What exactly is a generative model? Let's try to understand. In a simple way. Start with a pile of training photos.

Some images are likely, most are not, and a hidden rule decides which. That rule is the data distribution. Every training image is one draw from it. Picture a lottery over all images, where bedrooms win often and static almost never does.

A generative model is a machine with a lever. Each pull produces a fresh image. Training tunes its knobs, called parameters, until the draws look like the data. Concretely, a thirty two by thirty two color image is three thousand seventy two numbers, each from zero to two hundred fifty five.

The distribution covers all of them. How do we grade the machine? Yardstick one is likelihood: the probability the model gives real images it never saw. High probability means they do not surprise it.

seltz.snippet:
Most generative models try to learn a probability density. That sounds like the obvious goal, but it hides an awkward obstacle: the normalising constant. Score matching sidesteps it entirely by learning a different object, the gradient of the log-density, and that single change unlocks a family of models that includes modern diffusion models.

This article explains what the score is, why matching it is a sensible objective, how the practical estimators work, and where the idea breaks down.

## The problem with densities

Suppose we want to model data with an unnormalised density

p~(x;θ) \tilde{p}(x; \theta)

The true density is

p(x;θ)=p~(x;θ)Z(θ) p(x; \theta) = \frac{\tilde{p}(x; \theta)}{Z(\theta)}

where the partition function is

Z(θ)=∫p~(x;θ) dx Z(\theta) = \int \tilde{p}(x; \theta) \, dx

For any model beyond the simplest cases, that integral is intractable. Maximum likelihood therefore requires either a model class with a tractable normaliser, such as a normalising flow, or an expensive approximation, such as Markov chain Monte Carlo inside every training step.

Score matching asks a different question: what if we never need the normaliser at all?

## The score

s(x;θ)=∇xlog⁡p(x;θ) s(x; \theta) = \nabla_x \log p(x; \theta)

Here is the key observation. Take the log of the normalised density:

log⁡p(x;θ)=log⁡p~(x;θ)−log⁡Z(θ) \log p(x; \theta) = \log \tilde{p}(x; \theta) - \log Z(\theta)

The term log⁡Z(θ)\log Z(\theta) does not depend on xx , so it vanishes under differentiation:

A generative model learns to produce new examples that look like its training data, such as faces or photographs. ultimate.title: Denoising Is Stein: Moment Access and a Resource Hierarchy for Learning Hidden Structure in Diffusion Models
ultimate.snippet:
We study score learning from denoising pairs when the data contain a hidden non-Gaussian component. If covariance reveals the component, its subspace can be recovered directly. If covariance is isotropic, the first distinguishing moment has order $k^\ast$, and the learner must extract that moment from clean points and their noisy views.
Correlations in the denoising loss are Stein discrepancies against a baseline; for polynomial fields they determine exactly the corresponding moment differences. Averaging fresh noisy views conditional on a clean point gives an exact moment query on the clean distribution. In the covariance-matched regime, orientation-independent dictionaries satisfying an $L^4/L^2$ condition need order $d^{k^\ast-1}$ features, and the stated dot-product kernel ridge models need the same power in samples. Small-step online SGD on one unit has this exponent up to logarithms. A two-stage learner uses the curvature of a smoothed denoising loss to recover the hidden direction, then sharpens it and fits a scalar readout. For every even $k^\ast$, it obtains a fixed score gain over the Gaussian baseline from $O(d^{k^\ast/2}\log d)$ clean points. In the covariance-visible regime, the frozen-feature threshold occurs at $d^J/J!$, while projection onto principal components makes the fitted-model, score-risk and generated-law distributions independent of ambient dimension.
In the covariance-matched experiments, the measured partial-trace overlaps are consistent with the proposed spectral transition. A width-8 network trained with clean-point reuse shows a $d^2$-like training-set threshold over $d=64$--$192$, with fixed validation and calibration overhead.

ultimate.snippet:
Diffusion models estimate the score $\nabla\log p_{t}$ as Gaussian noise progressively obscures a data distribution (Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021). Training provides __denoising pairs__ $(X_{0},X_{t})$: a clean point and a noisy view. The learner predicts $X_{0}$ from $X_{t}$, thereby estimating the score (Vincent, 2011). If the data have a hidden non-Gaussian direction, a successful denoiser must detect it through those pairs. The amount of data needed depends on what the learner can represent and whether it can use repeated views of the same clean point.

The first informative moment has order $k^{\ast}\geq 3$, the __generative exponent__ of the latent law. This is non-Gaussian component analysis (Diakonikolas et al., 2017; Tan and Vershynin, 2018) seen through a diffusion model.

ultimate.title: Sum-of-squares lower bounds for Non-Gaussian Component Analysis
ultimate.snippet:
> Abstract:Non-Gaussian Component Analysis (NGCA) is the statistical task of finding a non-Gaussian direction in a high-dimensional dataset. Specifically, given i.i.d.\ samples from a distribution $P^A_{v}$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ that behaves like a known distribution $A$ in a hidden direction $v$ and like a standard Gaussian in the orthogonal complement, the goal is to approximate the hidden direction. The standard formulation posits that the first $k-1$ moments of $A$ match those of the standard Gaussian and the $k$-th moment differs. Under mild assumptions, this problem has sample complexity $O(n)$. On the other hand, all known efficient algorithms require $\Omega(n^{k/2})$ samples. Prior work developed sharp Statistical Query and low-degree testing lower bounds suggesting an information-computation tradeoff for this problem.
> Here we study the complexity of NGCA in the Sum-of-Squares (SoS) framework. Our main contribution is the first super-constant degree SoS lower bound for NGCA. Specifically, we show that if the non-Gaussian distribution $A$ matches the first $(k-1)$ moments of $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ and satisfies other mild conditions, then with fewer than $n^{(1 - \varepsilon)k/2}$ many samples from the normal distribution, with high probability, degree $(\log n)^{{1\over 2}-o_n(1)}$ SoS fails to refute the existence of such a direction $v$. Our result significantly strengthens prior work by establishing a super-polynomial information-computation tradeoff against a broader family of algorithms. As corollaries, we obtain SoS lower bounds for several problems in robust statistics and the learning of mixture models.

ultimate.title: how correlated latent variablesaccelerate learning with neural networks
ultimate.snippet:
Neural networks extract features from data using stochastic gradient descent (SGD). In particular, higher-order input cumulants (HOCs) are crucial for their performance. However, extracting information from the pth cumulant of d-dimensional inputs is computationally hard: the number of samples required to recover a single direction from an order-p tensor (tensor PCA) using online SGD grows as d^(p−1), which is prohibitive for high-dimensional inputs. This result raises the question of how neural networks extract relevant directions from the HOCs of their inputs *efficiently*. Here, we show that correlations between latent variables along the directions encoded in different input cumulants speed up learning from higher-order correlations. We show this effect analytically by deriving nearly sharp thresholds for the number of samples required by a single neuron to weakly-recover these directions using online SGD from a random start in high dimensions. Our analytical results are confirmed in simulations of two-layer neural networks and unveil a new mechanism for hierarchical learning in neural networks.

In this paper, we show that neural networks can learn efficiently from higher-order cumulants by exploiting correlations between the latent variables of type u⋅x corresponding to input cumulants of different orders.

webiq.title: Score Matching — papers and benchmarks | Papers with Code
webiq.snippet: Score matching fits a probabilistic model by matching the gradient of its log-density with respect to the data, the score, to that of the data distribution, which avoids computing the intractable normalizing constant of unnormalized and energy-based models. Hyvärinen (2005) showed that the objective can be rewritten using only the model's score and its derivatives. Denoising score matching (Vincent, 2011) instead regresses the score of noise-perturbed data, and sliced score matching uses random projections to scale to high dimensions. Song and Ermon turned the idea into score-based generative modeling: a noise-conditional network learns scores at many noise levels and samples are drawn with annealed Langevin dynamics.

webiq.title: [1907.05600] Generative Modeling by Estimating Gradients of the Data Distribution
webiq.snippet: We introduce a new generative model where samples are produced via Langevin dynamics using gradients of the data distribution estimated with score matching. Because gradients can be ill-defined and hard to estimate when the data resides on low-dimensional manifolds, we perturb the data with different levels of Gaussian noise, and jointly estimate the corresponding scores, i.e., the vector fields of gradients of the perturbed data distribution for all noise levels. Our models produce samples comparable to GANs on MNIST, CelebA and CIFAR-10 datasets, achieving a new state-of-the-art inception score of 8.87 on CIFAR-10.

webiq.title: [2610.42036] Learning Clean Generative Processes from Noisy Measurements
webiq.snippet: We study how to learn a generative model of clean images using only noisy observations. Diffusion processes and their generalizations to non-Gaussian noise require posterior predictions at every noise level. We first show that it is possible to learn these predictions from independent noisy views using Noise2Noise regression, but only at or above the noise level of the training data. To learn the predictions below that level, needed to generate clean images, we impose consistency: a prediction should equal its expectation after continuing the sampling process.

webiq.title: [2405.15625v2] Nonlinear denoising score matching for enhanced learning of structured distributions
webiq.snippet: We present a novel method for training score-based generative models which uses nonlinear noising dynamics to improve learning of structured distributions. Generalizing to a nonlinear drift allows for additional structure to be incorporated into the dynamics, thus making the training better adapted to the data, e.g., in the case of multimodality or (approximate) symmetries. Such structure can be obtained from the data by an inexpensive preprocessing step. The nonlinear dynamics introduces new challenges into training which we address in two ways: 1) we develop a new nonlinear denoising score matching (NDSM) method, 2) we introduce neural control variates in order to reduce the variance of the NDSM training objective.
